claim: A 1.2 m three-sided pod with an open top is a physical boundary against direct contact and against large droplets thrown sideways from a patient lying on the cot
law: Xie et al. 2007: droplets larger than 60 to 100 um fall before they evaporate over 2 m; exhaled at 1 m/s (breathing) they travel under 1 m, at 10 m/s (cough) more than 2 m (for a source about 1.5 m up). Straight-line screen from the mouth (FXS-CAL-001 section 5; mouth 720 mm up, A2), rays traced to the walls, the cot plane, the open top and the open foot end
check: The side walls stand 0.58 to 0.74 m from the mouth and the head wall 0.45 m (perpendicular): they stop 84.9 % of horizontal directions, where a cough or sneeze goes when the patient turns on their side, and 47.7 % of all directions; 22.4 % leave through the open top, 2.4 % through the open foot end and 26.4 % meet the cot and body. Lying on the back, a cough points up: all of a 30 deg cone round the vertical leaves through the top (100.0 %). The 11.6 mm slit at each angle joint was a direct path 0.45 m behind the head (independent review 2026-11-12: weak); now covered (F8). A boundary against contact and sideways large droplets only
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F8; FXS-CLM-001 (may claim); V1 at TRL 4 records splash marks

claim: The pod gives a measurable reduction in airborne particle exchange with the next bed (team assumption and decision gate)
law: Rooney et al. 2021 review: 'limited evidence to support the use of 2 metres physical distancing and partition screens within healthcare'; King et al. predicted halved deposition downstream of a partial partition in one direction only; Gilkeson et al. found partitions may raise exposure near the source and for simulated health workers; partitions should exceed the breathing zone (30 cm hemisphere in front of the face) of both users. Ching et al.: full curtains lowered the next-bed bioaerosol from 11,503 to 3,782 cfu/m3. Li et al. 2021: dividers cut face-to-face exposure 99 % but side by side only 22.6 % (p = 0.49). Closed curtains 'may reduce but not eliminate' transfer (Clinical Infectious Diseases 2022, ACP Hospitalist summary)
check: Particles under about 60 to 100 um follow the room air. A supine patient's breathing zone points up through the open top, so the pod does not exceed it (independent review 2026-11-12: quote corrected, King and Gilkeson added). The effect may be small, zero or negative where ward air runs along the beds; unproven, not promised. Only the decision-gate test against an unshielded baseline can show it; nothing is claimed until then
closed_by: V1 decision-gate test (FXS-VER-001); FXS-CLM-001 (may claim only after testing)

claim: Perforated lower band and open top keep passive airflow (team deck)
law: Opening areas from the model: open top 2.42 m2, open foot end 1.78 m2, 40 holes of 40 mm (0.05 m2) at 350 mm
check: The perforations are 1.2 % of the openings and sit below the cot top, so the top and the foot end do all the work; the band adds 40 sealed hole edges to clean and cuts the leaf where its self-weight load is highest. The airflow claim holds without the band; keeping or dropping a team feature is Amish's call
closed_by: Proposed, awaiting Amish: FXS-DEC-001 D4 (recommend drop)

claim: A person inside does not suffer heat build-up in a warm climate (metabolic heat 72 to 108 W)
law: ASHRAE Fundamentals metabolic rates (sleeping 72 W, reclining 81 W, seated 108 W for 1.8 m2, via the EnergyPlus reference); point-source plume G = 0.005 Q^(1/3) (y + d)^(5/3) (Kofoed and Nielsen 1988), whole heat taken as convective (A10, overstates the plume temperature), d 0.4 m, rise 0.4 m to the wall top
check: The plume carries about 51.9 to 59.4 m3/h out of the open top at 4.1 to 5.4 K above the ward: heat is not trapped under a lid. The point-source formula for a lying body is an estimate, and plume flow is entrainment, not a measured exchange of the pod (independent review 2026-11-12: weak). A febrile patient makes more heat. What the walls take away is sideways air movement (draught or fan) that cools a patient in a hot ward; that is S44
closed_by: V3 thermal comfort test at TRL 4 (FXS-VER-001)

claim: A patient lying in the pod is hidden from people walking past at 0.7 m or more from the wall
law: Sightline over a 1212 mm wall top: hidden depth b = a (h - z)/(e - h); ANSUR II standing eye heights 1,421 to 1,753 mm (NCSU); chest under bedding at 810 mm, face at 720 mm
check: At 1 m from the wall the chest is hidden for 0.74 to 1.93 m behind it and the face for 0.91 to 2.36 m, against 0.58 m to the face. A 95th percentile man sees the face from within 0.64 m of the wall, and in the 1.01 m gap between pods at a 2.5 m pitch people pass about 0.5 m from each wall, where the face is hidden only 0.46 m deep (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, restated). Visual privacy only, lying down, from most of the aisle

claim: The pod gives privacy to a patient sitting up on the cot
law: Seated eye height above the seat 698 to 860 mm (ANSUR II); seat on the cot canvas about 450 mm
check: Seated eyes are at 1148 to 1310 mm, -64 to +98 mm about the wall top: a seated patient's head is seen and sees out. The team claim fails as stated and is restated as privacy lying down; restating a user-facing claim is Amish's (independent review 2026-11-12: label corrected)
closed_by: Proposed, awaiting Amish: FXS-DEC-001 D3 (height and claim)

claim: Staff can observe the patient without entering the pod (team deck: semi-transparent upper panels)
law: Same sightline at 0.3 m from the wall; face 0.58 m from the wall; P12 has no upper panel
check: From the open foot end, everyone sees the patient. From the side, a staff member at 0.3 m from the wall sees the face only if tall: the hidden depth is 0.27 m for a 95th percentile man and 0.71 m for a 5th percentile woman. The team's semi-transparent upper panels are not in FS1; observation from the foot end only is a real limit on spotting a patient getting worse, so foot ends must face the nurse station (S50) (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, label corrected). Frosted or mesh panels need a P18 wall and their own fire report (X11)

claim: The pod fits cots 60 to 100 cm wide (team deck)
law: Inner width from the model; MSF field hospital bed 190 to 200 x 75 to 85 cm, lying surface 50 to 55 cm; NATO style camp bed 190 x 64 x 40 cm; US style military cot 78 x 28 x 18 in; hand and bedding gap 75 mm a side (A9)
check: Inner width 1170 mm at the folds, 1483 mm at the joints: gaps of 285, 210, 160 and 85 mm a side for cots of 600, 750, 850 and 1,000 mm, so the widest cot fits with 85 mm. The fit is by clearance, not by adjustment; no staff member can stand inside beside any of them (S21)

claim: The pod covers a cot 190 to 200 cm long
law: Side wall 1913 mm from the head line; cot head 260 mm from it
check: A 1.9 m cot overhangs the open end by 247 mm and a 2.0 m cot by 347 mm: head and body are inside, the feet outside

claim: The pod does not tip when pushed from the aisle with the 178 N BIFMA X5.6 force
law: FXP-PLT-001 P6, P7 method: rigid-body tipping about the outrigger tips, push at 1110 mm (102 mm below the top); masses from the model with four 5 kg bags (26.0 kg standing)
check: As one rigid body the pod would hold 239 N, but it is not one: the zigzag side wall is soft in torsion and a 600 mm leaf bows 25 mm at 5.8 N (FXP-PLT-001 P4). Locally the free end of a side wall tips at about 11 N. The bag sits 135 mm inside the outrigger tip, so it adds little against outward tipping (independent review 2026-11-12: holds). Proposed fix: state the platform limit L1 (a boundary that tips if leant on) with a lower lateral criterion; more ballast does not close it
closed_by: Proposed, awaiting Amish: FXS-DEC-001 D5 (with FXP-PLT-001 D5)

claim: A patient can pull on a panel to sit up or stand, or roll against it, without the pod tipping or folding onto them (fall risk)
law: Hand load in sit-to-stand with a handle 20 to 41 % of body weight (Bolli et al., one young adult; a frail patient loads the hands more); 70 kg patient (A1); ADA 609.8 asks a grab bar for 1112 N
check: Needs 137 to 281 N. A side wall pulled inward tips locally at about 9 N (a released half at 16 N) and a 600 mm leaf bows 25 mm at 5.8 N, so it gives way and the patient falls; a patient rolling in rigors or delirium against a wall 0.2 m away does the same, and field cots have no rails, so the wall looks like one (independent review 2026-11-12: holds; the sign is the weakest control and does not close it). Fixed now: an ISO 3864 prohibition sign with the words 'Do not lean or pull. Ask staff to help you stand.' on both side walls at 700 to 900 mm (F2). Whether the pod may be used for patients who need support to stand, are delirious or are children is a scope and safety decision
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F2 (standing instruction); Proposed, awaiting Amish: FXS-DEC-001 D2

claim: The pod does not slide when bumped
law: Friction mu W of the standing pod; EPDM pad on wet to dry vinyl or tent floor mu 0.4 to 0.6 (ASSUMED, A4, to measure; wet EPDM on vinyl may be lower; FXP-PLT-001 D17)
check: Slides at 102 to 153 N as a whole, so the 178 N push may slide it, more so on a wet floor; a half alone tips (about 22 N) before it slides (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, restated). A pod that slides moves toward the next bed
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F4 (pads, standing instruction); T7 at TRL 4

claim: Clips hold the joints while a patient pulls on a wall
law: FXP-PLT-001 P9: 176 N per clip on paper (pull-out of two through-pegs), not bounded by test. A pull at 900 mm shared by the head corner fold and the side joint; at the joint the top clip (1,062 mm) takes 82 % by lever arm
check: About 56 to 115 N on the top clip if the fold takes half, 113 to 231 N if the joint takes it all, which passes the paper capacity at the high end; the load is also out of plane (prying) (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, lever arm added). The wall gives way first (S11)

claim: The platform angle clip takes a panel in both of its slots
law: Interference check of the model (cad_check.py) with fx.clip('angle') as the platform helper builds it: square 12 mm core, panel edge stopped at 6 mm from the joint line by the hole pattern
check: As built, the square core stands 6 / cos 30 = 6.93 mm from the axis in the 150 deg slot, 0.93 mm proud of the stop line, so a panel cut to the platform hole pattern overlapped the core by 147 mm3 and its holes missed the pegs by 0.93 mm against 0.5 mm of clearance (fails as built). Fixed: the same arms on a 12 mm round core (F1); platform request 1
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F1 (standing instruction); REVIEW platform request 1

claim: Each outrigger carries the tipping load into its foot block
law: FXP-PLT-001 section 5.4 describes the folded outrigger but not how it is held to the block. Inward tipping loads the beam as a cantilever under its 5 kg bag: M = 6.4 N m; skins-only thin triangle I = a^3 t / 4 = 16250 mm4 (t = 2 x 0.26 mm)
check: A beam that only butts against the block carries no moment, so the outrigger did nothing as drawn. Fixed: a 100 mm triangular spigot on the block, the beam slid over it and a 6 mm stainless pin across both (F3). Bending stress about 11.3 MPa against a raw PP yield of 24 MPa (FXP-PLT-001), so a factor of about 2 before local buckling of the 0.26 mm apex skin, which crush scoring weakens; pin bearing on two skins unproven (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, numbers added)
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F3 (standing instruction); T7 at TRL 4; REVIEW platform request 2

claim: The terminal leaf at each open end stands under its own weight, cold and hot
law: FXP-PLT-001 P2 Greenhill flat strip, h_cr 1,441 mm cold and 1,144 mm hot: at 1,200 mm (h_cr / H)^3 = 1.73 cold and 0.87 hot. These are raw factors with no load factor (platform_check.py line 143); a leaf with one free edge and no twisting stiffness buckles like that strip. With both edges held, FXP-PLT-001 P3 gives 4.7 cold and 2.4 hot at 1,200 mm, load factor 2 included
check: First drawn with a free edge, the leaf would buckle in a hot tent (0.87) and creep toward it over weeks (independent review 2026-11-12: refuted; the author had read 1.73 as including a factor of 2). Fixed: an aluminium edge channel bolted over each free edge (F7), so the leaf is held on both edges; with creep at 0.3 of the short-term stiffness (reviewer's estimate) the margin is about 1.4 with the load factor of 2 still in it
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F7 (standing instruction); FXP-PLT-001 T1 hot; REVIEW platform request 3

claim: Staff can open the pod for resuscitation within seconds (team risk; platform first-order check)
law: ERC 2021 BLS: 'Start chest compressions as soon as possible' and 'on a firm surface whenever feasible'; ILCOR 2024: firm surface when practical, moving a patient to the floor judged not worth its risks. Release: two clips at the head centre (two fingertips on two lips each, crouching for the low one), then both head leaves swing 90 deg outward on their corner folds (A8)
check: As first drawn (slide one half 0.8 m) the half, with two 5 kg bags on it, tips at about 22 N before it slides at about 50 to 75 N, so it fell over instead: 30 to 60 s or a dropped wall (independent review 2026-11-12: refuted). Fixed (F5): no foot at the head centre, so after the two clips are released the head leaves swing open on their folds with nothing lifted or slid: about 8 to 20 s, a 0.85 m opening on each side of the head. It needs 0.6 m clear behind the head wall to swing and to reach the clips (F9). For full access the occupied cot is pulled about 1.1 m out of the open foot end (1483 mm wide). A field cot's canvas is not a firm surface in any case
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F5, F9 (standing instruction); V2 timed release at TRL 4

claim: Staff reach the patient for routine care without moving a panel
law: Side gap 210 mm for a 0.75 m cot; wall top 1212 mm; cot top 500 mm
check: Fails: nobody stands beside the cot inside the pod, and reaching over a 1.2 m wall to a patient 0.6 m in is poor practice for handling. Routine care is from the open foot end, or with the head opened (S17), or with the cot set off centre to give one 345 mm working side. Changing the pod's width changes the plan and the bed spacing

claim: A patient can get out of the pod quickly, including in a fire
law: Open foot end 1483 mm wide at the joints and 1170 mm at the folds; side gap 210 mm; FXP-PLT-001 section 9 keeps the open end clear
check: A walking patient sits on the cot's foot end and steps out of the open end, climbing over the cot end rail that stands 247 mm out; nothing latches. Staff can pull the occupied cot straight out of the open end, which is wider than any cot in range ({REV}: holds, cot pull added). The narrow side gap makes sitting on the side edge awkward (falls risk); the off-centre cot of D6 helps
closed_by: V2 egress drill at TRL 4; FXS-DEC-001 D6

claim: FR twinwall panels round a sleeping patient and bedding are an acceptable fire case
law: FXP-PLT-001 P23 and FR1 (27.8 MJ/m2; FR delays ignition, does not reduce fire load); PET 21.4 MJ/kg (UQ) for printed parts and bags; solid foam mattress with FR cover 7.3 kg, 19.7 MJ/kg, peak 917 kW (CBUF item 1:21, NCFS table, an upper value); point-source radiation with a radiative share of 0.3 (ASSUMED, A5); Heskestad flame height L = 0.235 Q^(2/5) - 1.02 D; PP ignited and burned in the cone at 25 kW/m2 (FSRI)
check: The pod adds 201 MJ (165 MJ of sheet) beside a 144 MJ mattress, 1.4 times the bed's own load. The mattress flame is about 2.2 m high, so walls 0.2 to 0.4 m away stand in or against it and will burn, melt and drip whatever their grade; three walls also re-radiate onto the bed and channel the flame. NFPA 701 TM1 (the platform minimum, a curtain test) does not show behaviour beside a burning bed (independent review 2026-11-12: holds, stronger by flame height). Rules now: pods never touch (F6), no heat sources, lamps, candles, coils or chargers in or on a pod. No fix within the principle makes this acceptable on paper: the benchmark, a full-scale bed-and-pod test and whether the risk is accepted are Amish's, with the site's fire safety staff
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F6 (standing instruction); Proposed, awaiting Amish: FXS-DEC-001 D7 (with FXP-PLT-001 D18)

claim: Pods next to each other do not carry a fire from bed to bed
law: Bed centre spacing 2.5 m in general wards (Bettercare IPC facility design, section 5-5); pod width 1.487 m on its joints; same point-source screen for the mattress
check: At a 2.5 m pitch the neighbour's wall stands 1.76 m from the burning bed's centre line, where the mattress alone gives about 7.1 kW/m2. The larger threat is the burning pod's own 1.9 x 1.2 m walls, 1.01 m from the neighbour's wall: the reviewer estimates 15 to 25 kW/m2 there (view factor about 0.25, emissive power assumed) (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, distances corrected). Closer pitches make it worse. Spacing is a site rule set with fire safety staff (D7)
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F6; D7; T8 at TRL 4

claim: Oxygen given to a patient inside a pod does not raise the fire risk
law: Messer safety alert: oxygen-enriched air is more than 23.5 % O2; bedding and clothing enriched with oxygen become 'extremely flammable'. Excess oxygen at 5 to 15 L/min (ASSUMED, A14), 93 to 100 % purity, mixed into the plume exchange flow of S4, and into half of it
check: Bulk pod air reaches 21.3 to 22.2 % with the full exchange and up to 23.6 % at 15 L/min with half of it, at the 23.5 % threshold. Oxygen is denser than air and soaks into bedding, so local enrichment at low level inside three walls is the real hazard (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, quantified). Rule now: no cylinders or concentrators inside or fixed to the pod; tubing taken out over the nearest wall top, clear of the head release joint (F6); oxygen patients in a pod only after the site's fire review
closed_by: FXS-DEC-001 F6; site fire review (release limitation)

claim: Smoke from the FR sheet is no worse than other FR plastics in a sleeping space
law: FXP-PLT-001 P37 and D11: brominated FR with antimony trioxide; combustion products include hydrogen bromide and antimony oxides
check: To assess with the halogen-free FR question; a sleeping patient is the worst case for smoke exposure

claim: One person with no training deploys the pod around a cot in under 5 minutes (team deck)
law: Step count from the model (4 feet with pre-pinned outriggers and bonded pads, 4 duos, 6 clips, 4 filled bags, one check) x ASSUMED action times (A7)
check: 4.2 to 8.3 min with the bags already filled and staged and the cot empty: the fast end meets 5 min, the slow end does not. Filling 20 kg of sand is a separate depot task. Around an occupied cot the cot is pulled about 0.5 m forward and back, a two-person handling task with a line-pull risk (independent review 2026-11-12: weak). One person can do the rest because a folded duo stands alone as an L before it is clipped

claim: All panels stack to 10 cm or less for storage (team deck)
law: FXP-PLT-001 section 11: a folded duo is about 10 mm thick; four duos
closed_by: Feet, outriggers and clips pack in the bag pocket (BOM item 9)

claim: One person carries the folded pod kit
law: Carried mass from the model with bags empty (A6); NIOSH load constant 23 kg as a ceiling only (FXP-PLT-001 P16)
closed_by: PR-011; 25 kg of sand filled on site, never carried (FXP-PLT-001 B1)

claim: Panels, clips, feet, pins and channels tolerate 0.5 % hypochlorite and 70 % alcohol wipes
law: FXP-PLT-001 P18 to P20 for PP and PETG; EPDM, stainless and aluminium not on those charts
check: Pins and bolts changed from A2 to A4 (316) stainless for repeated hypochlorite wipes; PETG tongues under strain may craze with alcohol (stress cracking); aluminium channels are rinsed after chlorine (independent review 2026-11-12: weak, A4 adopted). All to the T4 coupons

claim: Every surface facing the patient can be wiped
law: FXP-PLT-001 rules E1 to E3; back-face fold grooves; 40 perforation holes; the angle-joint slits
check: Print faces (no grooves) face the patient in both halves, so every groove faces the aisle (E2); the 11.6 mm joint slits are covered by strips that come off with the clips for cleaning (F8); hot-punched hole seals cannot be checked by eye, and FDM layer lines and clip interiors are crevices, so clips and channels come off for cleaning (E3) (independent review 2026-11-12: weak). Seal integrity under wiping unproven; the perforations add 40 sealed edges (D4)

claim: Folds and clips survive 50 deployments
law: FXP-PLT-001 P13 and P14: the 13.6 mm groove folds to 180 deg (3.4 % skin strain) and 90 deg either way; FS1 folds 60 and 30 deg in use
check: Inherited; the 60 deg corner fold is inside the platform's range

claim: The prototype pod's parts cost about USD 214, against the USD 120 value-engineering target
law: Priced BOM (bom/bom.csv), cited prices checked 2026-11-12; printed parts at filament cost
check: USD 214.00, USD 94.00 over the target (a value-engineering target, not a limit, STANDARDS 18); drivers sheet USD 90, freight share USD 25 and carry bag USD 20. The cash outlay for a first prototype is about USD 600 (minimum 10 sheets plus freight), shared across pods (independent review 2026-11-12: holds, cash added). The USD 75 stretch is not shown

claim: Pods fit a ward without losing many beds
law: Footprint from the model: outriggers 300 mm out each side, the cot end of a 2.0 m cot and 0.6 m clear behind the head (F9); MSF cholera guideline about 4 m2 per bedridden patient and 10 beds plus a nurse station per 45 m2 tent; general ward bed pitch 2.5 m (Bettercare); half a 1.2 m foot-end aisle per pod (A11)
check: Each pod needs 2.09 x 2.86 m (5.97 m2), 7.22 m2 with its aisle share: about 6.2 pods in a 45 m2 tent against 10 plain beds, about 38 % fewer (independent review 2026-11-12: refuted at 'a quarter'; the cot end had been left out). At a 2.5 m pitch the walls fit with 413 mm between outrigger tips at floor level (S41); in surge wards at a tighter pitch they do not

claim: The pod is for use indoors or inside a tent
law: FXP-PLT-001 P8 and limit L2
check: Inherited

claim: Patients accept the pod and do not find it isolating (team risk)
law: Open top and foot end; seated patients see out (S6); no cited study of partial enclosures in field wards found
check: To assess with patients and humanitarian health practitioners

claim: Warning and release marks are read correctly
law: FXP-PLT-001 C1 to C3: colour never the only code; safety colours keep their ISO 3864 meanings; ISO 7010 symbols where registered, ISO 3864-3 for custom ones
check: First drawn as a yellow band, but 'Do not lean or pull' is a prohibition, which ISO 3864-1 draws as a red circle and bar (independent review 2026-11-12: refuted). Now a prohibition sign (red circle and bar on white, custom pictogram to ISO 3864-3) with the words in black on white; release marks are black and white with words, not red; words in local languages. Comprehension unproven

claim: Ballast does not bring wet or soiled bags onto a clinical floor
law: FXP-PLT-001 rule B1; 25 kg of sand per pod
check: Bags filled with clean sand off the clinical floor, closed and wiped; a sealed wipeable bag to source (C3)

claim: Edges, grooves, folds and joints do not cut or pinch hands, including the patient's
law: FXP-PLT-001 P34; slit at a 150 deg angle joint 2 x 6 x sin 75 = 11.6 mm, opening and closing as the wall racks; the reviewer cites 8 to 25 mm as a finger-entrapment band (ISO 13857, EN 1176; not checked here)
check: The slits were a finger trap within reach of a patient 0.2 m away (independent review 2026-11-12: weak). Fixed: cover strips on both faces (F8). Sealed edges and folds as the platform

claim: Static charge on PP panels is acceptable next to oxygen and monitors
law: FXP-PLT-001 P33 (Interprofile antistatic grade 1e9 to 1e12 ohm/sq on request; standard PP highly insulating)
check: Standard PP charges in dry tents; a discharge near oxygen-enriched bedding is a low-probability ignition source that is not argued away here (independent review 2026-11-12: weak). Anti-static FR grade availability to assess

claim: The pod supports IPC practice; it makes no claim on airborne transmission
law: STANDARDS 25.5b; S1 and S2
check: Claims limited to a physical boundary against contact and sideways large droplets, privacy lying down and a clear bed space (FXS-CLM-001)

claim: The angle-joint slits do not break privacy or let droplets through
law: Slit 2 x 6 mm x sin 75 deg = 11.6 mm wide between and beyond the 100 mm clips at three joints, about 0.03 m2 in all
check: A sightline and a droplet path 0.45 m behind the head as drawn first (missed claim). Fixed: flexible clear PP cover strips on both faces in three lengths per joint, heat-staked to one leaf so the head joint still releases (F8)

claim: The free ends of the side walls stand in a tent with the door open or a fan running
law: q = 0.5 rho v^2 on the two 0.6 x 1.2 m leaves of a side duo, rho 1.2 kg/m3; free end tips at about 11 N (S10)
check: Gusts of 2, 3 and 5 m/s give 3.5, 7.8 and 21.6 N, so a door gust or a pedestal fan aimed at a pod can tip a free end (missed claim). Placing pods away from tent doors and fans, or more ballast at the free ends, changes the site rules

claim: The aisle between pods stays clear for staff, stretchers and escape
law: At a 2.5 m bed pitch: walls 1.01 m apart, outrigger tips with their bags 413 mm apart at floor level; cot overhang into the foot aisle 0.25 to 0.35 m
check: A 43 mm outrigger and a 70 mm bag at the floor are trip edges for staff carrying patients or buckets, and the clear floor between pods is narrow (missed claim). Outriggers and bags marked on the floor; side aisles are not escape routes; the foot aisle width is a site rule (D8)

claim: Staff working at the open foot end are not exposed more than at an open bed
law: Rooney et al. 2021: partitions may raise exposure near the source and for simulated health workers (Gilkeson, Nielsen)
check: The foot end is where staff stand, in the pod's plume and slower air (missed claim). Unknown sign and size; PPE practice unchanged
closed_by: V1 measures at the staff position at TRL 4

claim: The pod works with mosquito nets over the cot (malaria settings)
law: Treated nets hang over and are tucked under cots; side gap 210 mm for a 0.75 m cot
check: Hanging and tucking a net inside a 1.2 m wall with a 210 mm gap is awkward, and a net adds fire load beside the bedding (missed claim). To check with field partners
closed_by: V4 with field partners at TRL 4

claim: Patients in a hot ward lose no cooling from fans or draughts
law: Walls 0.2 m from a lying patient block sideways air movement; the reviewer quotes about 2 to 3 K of comfort credit for 0.8 m/s air (ASHRAE 55 practice, not checked here)
check: The main thermal effect of the pod is lost air movement, not trapped heat (missed claim). A ceiling fan still reaches the open top; a pedestal fan must blow into the open foot end (and S40 applies)

claim: Cholera cots and floor-level splash are compatible with the pod
law: Cholera beds carry a bucket under the bed (MSF cholera guideline); feet, outriggers, bags and the 350 mm perforated band sit in the splash zone
check: Daily chlorine mopping goes round four feet and four bags per pod, and bags soak up liquid (missed claim). For cholera use, bags in sealed wipeable covers (C3) and no perforated band (D4)

claim: The pod stands on uneven tent floors
law: Four rigid feet on a groundsheet over earth; 2 mm pads
check: A high spot of 10 mm unloads a foot and its bag and the pod rocks; tipping figures fall further (missed claim). Slope and step tolerance to measure
closed_by: T7 on a 1:50 slope at TRL 4

claim: Panels can be disposed of after an outbreak without harm
law: About 4 kg of brominated FR PP and 1.3 kg of PETG per pod; FXP-PLT-001 D11
check: Contaminated panels are often burned in pits or simple incinerators, which releases hydrogen bromide and may form brominated dioxins and furans (missed claim). End-of-life route to assess with the halogen-free FR question

claim: Carers, children, IV stands and lines fit the pod
law: Side gap 210 mm for a 0.75 m cot; walls tip at about 10 N
check: No room for a carer's mat or an IV stand inside; children will climb walls that tip; lines over a wall snag when the head opens (missed claim). IV stand outside at the foot end, lines kept off the walls and clear of the release joint; children in pods only by site rule
